notes:
I have gathered substantial material from across the approved sites. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes, drawing on each tradition as found.

---

## 1 Samuel 14:27–52 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 27 — Jonathan unknowingly breaks Saul's oath

Jonathan had not been present when Saul "made the people swear" (literally, "adjured the people"). He was already out pursuing the Philistines, having led the initial attack. In the heat of pursuit he dipped the end of his staff into a honeycomb and ate — and immediately his "eyes brightened," meaning his dimness from extreme exhaustion passed away and his strength was revived. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew written text (the *kethib*) reads "his eyes saw" rather than "his eyes were enlightened" — a poetic and forceful reading that most modern commentators prefer, though the Masoretic correction (*keri*) gives "became bright." (StudyLight.org Pulpit Commentary, v. 27)

Gill adds that honey, "being of a subtle nature, gives immediate refreshment and rigour," and notes that Jewish writers frequently use this phrase for refreshment after hunger, fatigue, and weariness. (BibleHub, Gill on v.27)

Benson (Methodist): "He was refreshed, and recovered his lost spirits. This cleared his sight, which was grown dim by hunger and faintness." (StudyLight.org, Benson on vv.27-28)

---

### v. 28 — A soldier informs Jonathan of the oath

One of the soldiers (apparently one who came with Saul's forces, now united with Jonathan's) told Jonathan that Saul had "straitly charged" — bound the troops with a solemn oath — cursing anyone who ate that day. The result: "the people were faint." The Pulpit Commentary notes there is diversity of opinion whether "and the people were faint" is part of the soldier's speech or the narrator's comment. It makes better sense as the continuation of the history, inserted to justify Jonathan's disapproval. The right rendering is "were weary." (StudyLight.org, Pulpit Commentary v.28)

---

### v. 29 — Jonathan's critique: "My father has troubled the land"

**Traditional reading (most Protestant commentaries):**

Jonathan speaks bluntly: "My father has troubled the land." Ellicott notes the Hebrew word for "troubled" here is *'akar*, the same root from which "Achan" and "Achor" come (Joshua 7:25-26) — equating Saul's foolish command with Achan's sin that troubled Israel. Ellicott paraphrases: "My father's ill-considered vow has done grave harm to us in Israel. Had he not weakened the people by hindering them from taking the needful refreshment, our victory would have been far more complete." (BibleHub, Ellicott on v.29)

Gill acknowledges the tension: "This was not wisely said by Jonathan; how much soever his father was to be blamed, it did not become him as a son thus to reflect upon him, and it might have tended to mutiny and sedition." Yet Gill also notes that Jonathan's point was objectively correct — the visible refreshment from just "a little of this honey" proved the folly of the fast. (BibleHub, Gill on v.29)

Dr. Constable (Evangelical): Jonathan "saw the folly of Saul's oath clearly because he wanted God's glory." Constable notes that Saul, not Jonathan, had troubled Israel, as Achan had. (StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.24-35)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (EnduringWord / David Guzik):** Jonathan was "exactly right." Saul had indeed troubled the land with his pseudo-spiritual command. "Because of his command, the people were faint on a day when they should have been strong. They were weak and distracted and the victory was diminished." (EnduringWord.com, section 2 on vv.25-30)

**Baptist (John MacArthur / GTY):** MacArthur highlights Jonathan's words — "this gave me some energy" — and his conclusion that the slaughter was "not nearly the victory that it could have been if we had been fed." MacArthur calls Saul's oath "a stupid thing" and "a ridiculous oath." (GTY.org, "Jonathan: The Man Who Would Not Be King")

---

### v. 30 — "How much better if the people had eaten freely"

Jonathan reasons: if a mere taste of honey so revived him, how much more would a full meal from the plunder have strengthened the whole army? The result would have been "a much greater slaughter among the Philistines." Gill comments: "The people would have had more strength to smite them, and would have pursued them with greater ardour and swiftness." Saul's own stated end — vengeance on his enemies — "would have been better answered by suffering the people to eat, than by forbidding them." (BibleHub, Gill on v.30)

Benson adds: "Thus men, by their rashness, hinder what they most desire." (StudyLight.org, Benson on v.30)

---

### v. 31 — The pursuit from Michmash to Aijalon

The Israelites struck down Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon — Aijalon being about 17 miles west of Michmash (Constable). The people were "very faint" from the exhausting, unremitting pursuit over steep terrain for hours, without food. (StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.24-35; EnduringWord citing Baldwin)

---

### v. 32 — The people sin by eating meat with the blood

When evening came and the oath's time limit expired, the famished soldiers "rushed greedily" (literally "flew upon") the spoil. In their ravenous hunger they slaughtered sheep, cattle, and calves on the ground and ate the meat with the blood still in it — a direct violation of God's law (Leviticus 17:10-14; Deuteronomy 12:23-25).

Benson: "Thus they who made conscience of obeying the king's commandment, for fear of the curse, made no scruple of transgressing God's command." (StudyLight.org, Benson on v.32)

**EnduringWord (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** "Their obedience to Saul's foolish command led them to disobey God's clearly declared command. This is always the result of legalism. We often think that legalistic rules will keep people from sinning, but actually legalistic rules provoke people to sin." (EnduringWord.com, section 3 on vv.31-35)

**Baptist (MacArthur):** "When they are allowed finally to eat, they gorge themselves because they're famished, and they eat meat mixed with blood... Everything this guy does is wrong." (GTY.org)

**Reformed (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown):** The army "were defiled by eating blood, or living animals." JFB notes the soldiers "were painfully conscientious in keeping the king's order for fear of the curse, but had no scruple in transgressing God's command." (BibleHub, JFB on vv.31-34)

---

### v. 33 — Saul hears of the sin and commands a stone be rolled

Someone reported to Saul that the troops were "sinning against the LORD." Saul's first word — "You have broken faith" (or "Ye have transgressed") — shows, as Benson notes, that "he sees their fault, but not his own, in giving the occasion of it." (StudyLight.org, Benson on vv.33-34)

Saul ordered a large stone rolled to serve as a slaughtering table. Constable notes this was "a slaughtering table where the priests carefully prepared the meat for eating," ensuring the blood could drain properly. (StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.24-35)

---

### v. 34 — Saul organizes proper slaughter

Saul dispersed officers to instruct the troops: each man must bring his ox or sheep to this central stone, slaughter it there properly, and only then eat. "Do not sin against the LORD by eating meat with the blood." That night, the people complied. The scene underscores that Saul was concerned with ritual observance even while failing to see his own culpability. Constable says Saul "showed great concern about the observance of religious rituals, but he failed to appreciate the indispensable importance of submitting his will to Yahweh." (StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.36-46)

---

### v. 35 — Saul builds his first altar to the LORD

The writer notes pointedly: "it was the first time he had built an altar to the LORD." Constable comments: "The writer's note that this was the first altar that Saul built reflects the king's general lack of commitment to Yahweh." He adds that Saul may have built this altar "simply to make amends for his legal infringement, not to express gratitude for the day's victory." Yet Saul was not entirely insensitive to Yahweh — his concern about the dietary law and his desire to honor God show some awareness. (StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.24-35)

**EnduringWord:** The altar may have been built on the large stone Saul had rolled, "using the stone as the altar." (EnduringWord.com)

---

### v. 36 — Saul proposes a night pursuit; the priest counsels consulting God

Flushed with victory, Saul proposed an all-night pursuit: "Let us go down after the Philistines by night and plunder them until dawn, leaving no man alive!" The troops — apparently accustomed to going along with Saul — replied, "Do what seems good to you."

But the priest (Ahijah) intervened: "We must consult God here." Benson explains that the priest "stood before the altar, and wished to remind them that it was dangerous to undertake any thing without God's direction." (StudyLight.org, Benson on vv.36-37)

Constable notes: "Evidently Saul would not have inquired of God if Ahijah had not suggested that he do so." (StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.36-46)

---

### v. 37 — God does not answer Saul

Saul inquired of God: "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will You give them into the hand of Israel?" But God did not answer him that day — "though the priest, it seems, often asked an answer, yet he received none" (Benson).

**Evangelical consensus:** God's silence was the key sign Saul should have heeded. Constable: "Probably God did not answer his prayer immediately because Saul wanted this information to vindicate himself rather than God." Saul thought God did not answer because someone had violated Saul's rule (v.24), "which he confused with God's Law, calling violation of it sin. Really, God did not answer him because Saul was disloyal to Yahweh." (StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.36-46)

**Baptist (MacArthur):** "He finally goes to a priest to seek some divine help, does Saul, and the Lord refuses to answer. Again, Saul takes no responsibility for his part in the actions. He blames this and that and the other." (GTY.org)

---

### v. 38 — Saul summons the leaders to investigate the "sin"

Saul assumed God's silence meant a hidden sin had occurred and called all the leaders ("chiefs") to investigate. Constable observes: "Saul thought God did not answer him because someone had violated his rule (1 Samuel 14:24), which he confused with God's Law, calling violation of it sin (cf. Joshua 7:14)." Saul saw the problem as someone else's violation rather than his own. (StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.36-46)

---

### v. 39 — Saul's rash oath: "Even if it is my son Jonathan, he must die!"

Saul swore "As surely as the LORD who saves Israel lives" that whoever had sinned would die — even if it was his own son Jonathan. "But not one of the troops said a word."

Benson calls this "a proof of Saul's rashness and folly, and of the violence and impetuosity of his temper." He notes that none of the soldiers who had seen Jonathan eat informed against him "because they were satisfied that his ignorance excused him; and from their great love to Jonathan, whom they would not expose to death for so small an offence." (StudyLight.org, Benson on v.39)

**EnduringWord:** "When the Urim and Thummim fell silent and God didn't answer Saul, that was a sign Saul should have heeded — but instead he made another foolish oath about Jonathan." (EnduringWord.com, High Points)

---

### v. 40 — Saul divides the people: Israel on one side, Saul and Jonathan on the other

Saul proposed a process to identify the guilty party by lot: all Israel on one side, himself and Jonathan on the other. The troops again replied passively: "Do what seems good to you."

Constable notes the troops had "gone along with Saul's requests thus far" but would soon draw the line. (StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.36-46)

---

### v. 41 — Saul casts lots using Urim and Thummim

Saul prayed to "the LORD, the God of Israel": "Why have You not answered Your servant this day? If the fault is with me or my son Jonathan, respond with Urim; but if the fault is with the men of Israel, respond with Thummim." The KJV reads "Give a perfect lot," which Benson explains as "O Lord, so guide the lot, that it may discover who is guilty in this matter, and who innocent." Jonathan and Saul were selected; the people were cleared. (StudyLight.org, Benson on vv.41-42)

Benson adds an important theological observation: "God so ordered the lot; not that He approved Saul's execration (v.24), or his oath that the transgressor should die (v.39), nor that He would expose Jonathan to death; but that Saul's folly might be chastised, when he saw what danger it had brought upon his eldest and most excellent son; and that Jonathan's innocence might be cleared." (StudyLight.org, Benson on vv.41-42)

---

### v. 42 — The lot falls on Jonathan

The lot narrowed between Saul and Jonathan, and Jonathan was selected. God identified Jonathan — not because Jonathan was guilty before God, but because he had technically violated Saul's command (though he had not violated God's command and was in fact executing God's will). (StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.36-46)

---

### v. 43 — Jonathan confesses: "I only tasted a little honey… and now I must die?"

Jonathan honestly confessed: he tasted "a little honey with the end of the staff." His question — "And now I must die?" — highlights the absurd disproportion between his unknowing, trivial act and the death penalty. The end of the verse in the Hebrew carries the sense: "Here I am; I must die!" (cf. GTY.org)

---

### v. 44 — Saul pronounces the death sentence on Jonathan

Saul declared: "May God punish me, and ever so severely, if you, Jonathan, do not surely die!" This is another rash oath from Saul, compounding the first one.

Benson offers a nuanced reading: "Saul, however, seems to have been influenced by a real fear of God, and certainly is to be commended for having a greater regard to his oath than to his kindred and natural affection." Yet Benson also cites an anonymous writer who argues that God's providence in all this was designed to teach Saul a lesson: "What better lesson then could God give to him, and to all of such hasty, precipitate tempers, than to bring him into the grievous strait of either breaking a solemn oath or putting his own son to death?" The people's rescue shows God never intended Jonathan to die. (StudyLight.org, Benson on vv.44-45)

**Reformed (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown):** Saul "was, like Jephthah [Judg 11:31, 35], about to put his son to death, in conformity with his vow. But the more enlightened conscience of the army prevented the tarnishing the glory of the day by the blood of the young hero, to whose faith and valor it was chiefly due." (BibleHub, JFB on v.45)

---

### v. 45 — The people rescue Jonathan

The people intervened decisively: "Must Jonathan die — he who accomplished such a great deliverance for Israel? Never! As surely as the LORD lives, not a hair of his head will fall to the ground, for with God's help he has accomplished this today."

**Key points across traditions:**

- **Benson (Methodist):** The people "oppose their oath to his, and swear he shall not die. They did not rescue him by violence, but by reason and resolution." Josephus adds that "they offered prayers to God that he would forgive Jonathan's sin." Benson suggests Saul may have been secretly relieved: "We may suppose Saul had not so perfectly forgot the relation of a father, but that he was willing enough to have Jonathan rescued, and well pleased to have that done which yet he would not do himself." (StudyLight.org, Benson on vv.44-45)

- **EnduringWord (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** There are "at least three reasons why it was right to spare Jonathan": (1) the oath and penalty were foolish and should never have been enforced; (2) Jonathan broke it in ignorance; (3) God's approval was evident from His great blessing on Jonathan — "he has worked with God this day." The people finally stood up to Saul's foolishness. (EnduringWord.com, section 6 on vv.45-46)

- **Constable (Evangelical):** The soldiers "recognized that Saul's rule about abstaining from eating was not divine law. They correctly saw that even though Jonathan had violated Saul's rule, he had obeyed God's order to drive Israel's enemies out of the land." (StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.36-46)

---

### v. 46 — Saul abandons the pursuit

Saul "gave up his pursuit" and the Philistines returned to their own land. The implication, as EnduringWord notes, is that "the victory might have been greater if not for Saul's foolish oath." Saul's preoccupation with Jonathan's eating "cost him a great victory over the Philistines" (Constable). (EnduringWord.com; StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.36-46)

---

### vv. 47-48 — Summary of Saul's military achievements

After assuming the kingship, Saul fought against Moab, Ammon, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. "Wherever he turned, he routed them." He also defeated the Amalekites, delivering Israel from plunderers.

**Benson:** "Saul took the kingdom — that is, resumed the administration of it, after he had, in a manner, lost it by the Philistines, who had almost got the entire possession of it, and enslaved Israel." He notes Saul fought defensively — repelling enemies and keeping them within their own limits. (StudyLight.org, Benson on vv.47-48)

**Constable:** "Saul was an active warrior and was effective to an extent due to his native abilities and God's limited blessing. He punished the enemies of Israel, which was God's will. Yet he did not subdue and defeat them all as David did." (StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.47-52)

**EnduringWord (Guzik):** "Saul's strength was broad but shallow. Because Saul was not a man after God's own heart and he did not have God's blessing above his own natural abilities, his strength was limited." (EnduringWord.com, section 7)

---

### vv. 49-51 — Saul's family and military leadership

Saul's sons: Jonathan, Ishvi (also called Abinadab, 1 Samuel 31:2; Benson notes Ishbosheth is omitted here because the writer intended to mention only those who went into battle and were later slain with Saul), and Malchishua. His daughters: Merab (firstborn) and Michal. His wife: Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz. His army commander: Abner, son of Ner, Saul's uncle. Saul's father Kish and Abner's father Ner were both sons of Abiel.

Constable notes that "the information concerning Saul's family members that the writer recorded here corresponds to other similar ancient Near Eastern texts. It was common to give this information as part of a summary of a king's accomplishments." (StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.47-52)

---

### v. 52 — Continual war with the Philistines; Saul's recruitment

"The war with the Philistines was fierce for all the days of Saul." Whenever Saul noticed any strong or brave man, he enlisted him. 

**Benson:** "When he saw any one behave well in battle, or of great strength, he took him into his band to be near to him on all occasions." (StudyLight.org, Benson on v.52)

**Constable:** "God would later bring valiant warriors to David as He had previously brought to Saul (1 Samuel 10:26), but Saul now had to select recruits by personally evaluating them. This is another indication of God's limited blessing on Saul. In contrast, hundreds of soldiers volunteered to serve with David. Saul established a standing army in Israel for the first time (cf. 1 Samuel 8:11)." (StudyLight.org, Constable on vv.47-52)

**EnduringWord:** The chapter closes showing Saul's apparent strength — his military campaigns, his family, his growing army — but this strength was "broad but shallow." (EnduringWord.com)

---

## Points of Difference Between Traditions

### On whether Jonathan was right to criticize his father publicly (v. 29)

- **Gill (Baptist, older):** Jonathan "was not wisely" to reflect on his father before the troops — it might have tended to mutiny and sedition. (BibleHub, Gill on v.29)
- **EnduringWord (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** Jonathan "was exactly right" — speaking truth to power when Saul's foolishness was harming God's people. (EnduringWord.com)
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** Jonathan's zeal to defend himself "makes him run into the other extreme of accusing his father." (BibleHub, Ellicott on v.29)

### On Saul's motivation in sentencing Jonathan (v. 44)

- **Benson (Methodist):** Saul seems influenced by "a real fear of God" and is "to be commended" for regarding his oath above natural affection. Yet the whole episode was providentially designed to teach Saul the folly of rash oaths. (StudyLight.org, Benson)
- **Reformed/Baptist (MacArthur, Constable, JFB):** Saul is driven by "puny pride" (MacArthur). JFB compares him negatively to Jephthah. Saul's insistence on Jonathan's death shows him confusing his own commands with God's law. (GTY.org; StudyLight.org, Constable)
- **EnduringWord:** Saul's oath was never binding; the penalty itself was unjust, and God's silence was not about Jonathan at all but about Saul's own disqualification. (EnduringWord.com)

### On the significance of God's silence (v. 37)

- **Constable (Evangelical):** God did not answer "because Saul wanted this information to vindicate himself rather than God." (StudyLight.org)
- **Benson (Methodist):** God's silence was due to the sin of eating blood — yet Benson's anonymous source argues the whole sequence was divinely orchestrated to chasten Saul, not to expose Jonathan. (StudyLight.org, Benson)
- **EnduringWord (Pentecostal):** The silence was "a sign Saul should have heeded" — it was about Saul, not anyone else. (EnduringWord.com)

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (netbible.org notes, referenced in StudyLight.org extracts):** The NET Bible notes explain that "his eyes were enlightened" is a Hebrew idiom meaning "he was refreshed." The Pulpit Commentary contributes textual criticism: the written text (*kethib*) says "his eyes saw" rather than "his eyes became bright," a reading most modern commentators accept as more original and forceful. (StudyLight.org, Pulpit Commentary on v.27 and various)

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** No specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on these verses was found from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search limits. The standard Catholic approach to this passage typically follows the traditional reading, with Saul seen as a tragic figure whose rash religious zeal (comparable to Jephthah) leads him into conflict with natural law and the good of his son.

**On the lots / Urim and Thummim (v. 41):** The BSB translation ("respond with Urim… respond with Thummim") differs from the KJV's "Give a perfect lot." The Pulpit and other older commentaries work from the Hebrew text behind the KJV, while modern translations (following the Septuagint and other manuscript evidence) supply the explicit reference to Urim and Thummim. The older commentators (Benson, Gill) understood the casting of lots as a divinely guided process without necessarily specifying the mechanism.
